issues.legal_issue: A claimant cannot use retrospective payment of court fee to save a time-barred specific-performance claim when the plaint originally sought only an injunction and the fee was corrected only after a maintainability objection.
material_facts: The agreement fixed a date for performance, but the plaint was filed more than three years after that date.
The plaint sought a mandatory injunction directing transfer of the property, was valued as an injunction suit, and was accompanied by a fixed court fee.
Only after the respondent applied to dismiss the suit as not maintainable did the trial court treat it as a specific-performance suit and permit payment of the deficit fee.
The claimant paid the deficit fee but did not amend the plaint; the order permitting payment was not challenged.
issues.conclusion: Although Section 149 CPC ordinarily gives a permitted court-fee payment the same effect as payment at the outset, the claimant could not rely on it in these circumstances to avoid the consequences of having filed the specific-performance claim late in the form of an injunction suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 CPC permits a court, in its discretion, to allow payment of deficient court fee and gives that payment the same effect as if made initially. But a claimant seeking specific performance through a plaint framed only for injunction must seek amendment under Order VI Rule 17 CPC; an amendment may be refused as time-barred or may not relate back as a matter of course, as explained in K. Raheja Constructions Ltd. v. Alliance Ministries, Tarlok Singh v. Vijay Kumar, and Van Vibhag Karamchari Griha Nirman Sahkari Sanstha Maryadit v. Ramesh Chander. Specific performance is discretionary under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and Section 149 cannot be used in these circumstances to shelter the claimant’s approach.

rule.if: specific_performance_case and claim_filed_after_applicable_limit and injunction_only_relief_pleaded and correct_fee_paid_only_after_maintainability_objection

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding seeks, in substance, to compel performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.claim_filed_after_applicable_limit: The claimant filed the proceeding after the applicable time for bringing the specific-performance claim had expired.
predicates.injunction_only_relief_pleaded: The claimant initially framed the requested relief only as an injunction rather than seeking specific performance.
predicates.correct_fee_paid_only_after_maintainabil: The claimant paid the fee appropriate to the specific-performance claim only after the opposing party objected to the maintainability of the injunction suit.

issues.definition: When a late specific-performance claim is initially pleaded only as an injunction and the proper fee is paid only after a maintainability objection, the later fee payment does not save the claim.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who does not establish continuing readiness and willingness to perform the agreement is not entitled to discretionary specific performance, particularly where the claimant gives no explanation for a long delay in filing suit.
material_facts: The claimant issued a notice asserting readiness and willingness and relied on an affidavit said to show presence before the registering authority on the contractual performance date.
The claimant filed suit about three years after issuing the notice and gave no explanation for that delay.
The suit was initially framed as one for mandatory injunction and the trial court did not frame an issue on readiness and willingness.
issues.conclusion: The notice and affidavit did not establish that the claimant continued to be ready and willing when suit was filed; given the unexplained delay and the claimant’s conduct, the discretionary relief of specific performance was unavailable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires the claimant to aver and prove readiness and willingness to perform the essential contractual obligations. Readiness and willingness must be assessed from the claimant’s conduct, including whether it continued through the institution of the suit. Section 20 makes specific performance discretionary, and the court treated the unexplained delay and the limited evidence of readiness as material to that discretion.

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding seeks, in substance, to compel performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.readiness_evidence_confined_to_contract_: The claimant’s evidence of readiness and willingness relates only to the contractual performance date and does not establish continuation of that readiness when suit is filed.
predicates.unexplained_delay_after_notice: The claimant waits a substantial period after asserting readiness in a notice before filing suit and gives no explanation for the delay.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance proceeding, evidence limited to readiness on the contractual performance date, coupled with unexplained delay after notice, results in denial of discretionary specific performance.
